catalog_quote: Boyd (1989a:202-203) describes tone systems in Kebi-Benue as follows: ‘All the Southern languages of the Mbum group (Adamawa A.6.C) also have two, but the remaining subgroups have three [tone levels]. This difference seems to be attributable to the raising of a high-low patterns to a supra-high level. Tupuri adds a fourth level; Ruelland (1977) describes a distribution indicating a split associated with vowel quality (height) on the one hand, and with the voicing feature of initial consonants on the other (suggesting the influence of neighbouring Chadic languages) ... After establishment of four levels, voicing contrasts are lost in some dialects.’ A comparative study of tone in Kebi-Benue requires synchronic studies of the tone systems. The transcription of tone in Boyd’s word lists has to be checked.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for stress is stated anywhere. The only suprasegmental statement covering Ndai/Galke is a group-level, second-hand one: Kebi-Benue (Mbum) languages are tone languages, with three tone levels in the Northern subgroup to which Galke belongs (two in the Southern Mbum languages); PHOIBLE 1348 accordingly lists H, M, L tones for Galke. Neither Elders 2006 nor any other opened source mentions word stress or accent for Ndai.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Elders adds that Boyd's tone transcriptions have yet to be checked and that no synchronic tone study of these languages exists.
new_statements.domain_note: Group-level statement about Kebi-Benue/Mbum tone systems, not Ndai-specific; Ndai is reached only by its classification (Northern Mbum, Dama-Galke). The Galke data used by Elders come from Lacroix 1962 and Boyd's 1974 word list.
new_statements.identity_note: Ndai is the autonym (said to be the word for 'cow'); Galke is the Fulfulde exonym, Pormi/Dai further names. Lacroix 1962 described 'Galke ⁿdáí' from two speakers at Tcholliré (Oct 1960); Mohammadou 1979 (per Elders 2006: 46) lists Galke dialects Biteki, Pormi, Mberka. All refer to ndai1238; the tone statement quoted is about the Kebi-Benue/Mbum group (Boyd 1989 via Elders 2006), with Ndai covered only as a member of the Northern (Dama-Galke) subgroup, not described individually.

new_statements.relation_note: Same content and type as the existing statement (Elders 2006 quoting Boyd 1989a:202-203: tone language, no stress statement), now read from Boyd's own text via snippets. Small refinement: Boyd's sentence reads 'the remaining subgroups (except Tupuri) have three', a clause the Elders quotation on record drops; Boyd's classification p. 185 confirms Galke sits in the Northern Mbum subgroup to which the three-level statement applies. All stress/accent hits in the volume ('stress-accent', 'pitch accent', 'accented syllable', 'Stress-accent is not a feature of Gur languages') belong to other chapters (Williamson ch. 1, Naden ch. 7 Gur, Kru, Ijoid, Cross River, Bantu); 'word stress', 'stress is',…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Boyd treats the whole Adamawa-Ubangi group as register-tone languages; the Northern and Central Mbum subgroups (which include Galke/Ndai, listed at p. 185 as 'A. Northern.. 2. Dama, Galke (Ndai)/Pormi, Kali') have three lexical tone levels, the Southern Mbum languages two, the third level arising from a high-low pattern raised to a suprahigh level. Nothing is said about word stress or accent for Galke or for Mbum; Galke is mentioned only in the classification (p. 185) and the source list (p. 186: 'Lacroix (1962) - Galke word list', 'Boyd (1974) - locations and word lists for Dama, Galke/Pormi..').
new_statements.exceptions: Tupuri is excepted from the three-level statement (it adds a fourth level); contour tones 'formed by conjoining two level tones' are widespread in the group (p. 204). The statement covers Galke only by subgroup membership, not by Galke data.
new_statements.identity_note: Boyd 1989 does not describe Galke itself; it places 'Galke (Ndai)/Pormi' with Dama and Kali in the Northern Mbum subgroup (p. 185) and lists Lacroix 1962 (Galke word list) and Boyd 1974 (word lists) as the sources (p. 186). The tone statement is about the Mbum subgroups as a whole and reaches Galke only through that classification. The sole primary description, Lacroix 1962 (Journal of African Languages 1(2): 94-121), remains unopened (no open copy found in earlier passes).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Boyd treats the Mbum-group languages as lexical-tone languages: Southern Mbum has two tone levels, the remaining subgroups (which include Northern Mbum, where Galke/Ndai is classified) have three, Tupuri four. Nothing is said about word stress or accent for Galke or for Adamawa group 6; the volume's stress-accent passages belong to other chapters (Gur ch. 7 etc.).
new_statements.exceptions: '(except Tupuri)': Tupuri has four levels; the three-level statement covers Galke only through its subgroup membership, not from Galke data (Boyd's Galke source is Lacroix 1962's word list).
new_statements.identity_note: Boyd 1989 does not describe Galke itself: Galke (Ndai)/Pormi appears only in his classification of the Mbum group (Adamawa 6), Northern branch, subgroup A.2 'Dama, Galke (Ndai)/Pormi, Kali' (pp. 185-186), with Lacroix 1962 (word list) and Boyd 1974 as its sources; the tone statement (sec. 9.3.5) is about subgroups, so it covers Galke by membership only.

sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent anywhere. Sec. 3.4 Tone (pp. 58-63) opens by quoting Boyd 1989a: 202-203: Southern Mbum languages have two tone levels, 'the remaining subgroups have three' (Galke is Northern Mbum, Dama-Galke); the four tone topics treated are the verb, Tupuri, Mundang and Mono, not Galke. Galke data come from Lacroix 1962 and Boyd's 1974 word list (p. 49: 'data for Galke/Pormi, Pam/Mono, Dama and Kali are from Boyd's comparative word list'); Lacroix 1962: 104-105 is cited for the a- nominal prefix and free vs. linked noun forms (pp. 66, 71).
